content.text:
I submitted **part-based** with confidence 0.82, after spending 33 of the 60 budget.

**Design:** I trained the learner on just two tasks with no rules in common, `L1-S1-M1` and `L2-S2-M2`. That left every trained rule seen exactly once. Under factor-when-justified, a rule needs at least 2 trained tasks before it becomes a reusable part, so at this point that learner should behave exactly like the holistic one. I then compared two kinds of new task:
- **Recombinations** (`L2-S1-M1`, `L1-S2-M2`): no new rules, but they give the same response as the trained tasks on 0% of inputs.
- **Novel tasks** (`L3-S3-M4`, `L4-S4-M4`): all three rules new, and 6–19% overlap with the trained tasks.

**Results (examples needed to reach criterion):**

| Task type | New rules | Overlap with trained tasks | Mean | Tests |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Recombinations | 0 | 0% | ~21.5 | 13 |
| `L1-S3-M1` | 1 | 62.5% | ~27 | 5 |
| Novel | 3 | 6–19% | ~43.6 | 10 |
| Before any training | — | — | ~35 | 3 |

The recombinations took about half as many examples as the novel tasks, a difference of roughly 3.5 standard errors. Holistic and factor-when-justified (before any rule has been seen twice) both predict that zero-overlap recombinations should be no cheaper than novel tasks. Instead, cost went up with the number of new rules: 0, then 1, then 3.

**Caveats:**
- Test results were very noisy: one recombination ranged from 1 to 46 across repeats.
- Factor-when-justified is ruled out only because no rule had been trained twice. I didn't run the second stage (training rules a second or third time) that would have tested it directly.
- The `L1-S3-M1` test mixes one new rule with high overlap, so it doesn't separate the two explanations by itself.
